line:
I wipe the ink off my boots, pocket the map, keys and note, and say, "H.? That can't be Hale, he's in a cellar in Thornhallow." I decide to keep the packet for now and show it to the arbiter only after I've seen the Wick-House myself, since an "H." who watches doors might also have friends in the hall.

Then I bolt the door, put Kit on the first watch, eat a hot supper sent up by Bess, and take my long rest, planning to be at the quay before the dawn bell.

input.add_to_description: Day 9 evening: Wren holds Corvin's map (Wick-House circled, seaward end of the quay), three keys (brass, iron, small bent) and a note 'The keeper sleeps till dawn bell. H. watches the east door.' She told no one at the hall. Day 10 ~4 AM she woke from a long rest, planning to watch the quay before the dawn bell.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Wick-House

You say it aloud as you wipe the ink from your boots: "H.? That can't be Hale." Kit only shrugs. The packet goes into your pack, and you tell no one at the hall. A friend of Hale's, or of someone else's, could be anywhere on a quay, and a hall full of clerks is a good place to hear a secret and sell it.

You bolt the door. Bess sends up a hot supper of fish pie and bread, and you pay a silver for it. Kit takes the first watch on a stool by the door, her sword across her knees, and you sleep.

Nothing disturbs you. The night passes quietly, and Kit wakes you for your turn and then sleeps herself, both of you easier for it. You wake at about four in the morning, rested. You have all your hit points, all three first-level slots, and Bardic Inspiration at three. Best of all, the exhaustion has lifted by a level to 1, with only the disadvantage on ability checks left. Kit stirs and hears the news with a grunt. A second night's rest would clear it entirely.

The window is black, with a thin grey line along the sea. A few gulls are already crying. Down on the quay a lantern swings, and one door-shaped shadow stands very still at the east end of it, near the building you circled on Corvin's map. The dawn bell is a couple of hours off.

What does Wren do?

Bess sends up a hot supper of fish stew and bread, and you eat it with the packet tucked inside your psalter. You bolt the door and Kit takes the first watch, sitting on her bedroll with her sword across her knees. You sleep hard.

The night passes with nothing worse than gulls and a drunk singing on the quay. You wake in the dark before dawn, rested. Your spell slots are back, your three Bardic Inspirations are back, and Kit is fit and fed. I'll check whether the long rest has eased the exhaustion on your sheet. It is just after four in the morning on Day 10, and the dawn bell is still some way off.

You said Hale is in a cellar at Thornhallow, and that is what you were told. But "H." may be someone else, or Hale may have friends. The map shows the Wick-House near the seaward end of the quay, with an east door where someone watches. Corvin's note says the keeper sleeps until the dawn bell. His three keys are on the ring: one brass, one iron, one small and bent.

The quay is dark and the tide is turning. What does Wren do?

You wipe the ink off your boots and pocket the map, the three keys and the note. "H.? That can't be Hale," you tell Kit. "He's in a cellar at Thornhallow." Kit shrugs. "A man can have more than one friend who smiles." You decide the packet stays with you until you've seen the Wick-House yourself, since a watcher at one door may have friends in the hall.

You bolt the door. Bess sends up a hot supper of fish stew, bread and a jug of small beer, with a look that says she still isn't sure whose side she's on. You eat all of it. Kit takes the first watch on the stool by the door with her sword across her knees, and wakes you for nothing.

The night passes quietly. Once there are boots on the landing, and they stop outside Corvin's old room and then go away. Kit logs it in her flat way and says no more.

When you wake it's a little before dawn, and the gulls are starting up. The wet-wool weight of the last days has eased, though not gone. You and Kit are both still a little exhausted, with one level of it left, and you're otherwise whole: hit points full, all three spell slots back, Bardic Inspiration at three.

The dawn bell hasn't rung yet. The quay is grey outside the window, and the Wick-House is at its seaward end.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
